name: hard-gate-fires
description: A freight-domain backend role built on the Microsoft stack. The persona's domain preferences all match -- logistics is their strongest positive -- and the role is remote, backend, and IC. The only thing wrong with it is the stack, which is a hard gate. This is the enforced counterpart to the unit tests: it proves a gate still fires, is reported as its own kind of finding, and is not quietly downgraded into an ordinary conflict, through the same path RunFitEvaluation uses.
comment: The gate has been through two representations. It first contributed nothing at all, so a JD like this one read as though the exclusion had never been recorded; it was then priced into preference_score with a penalty and a ceiling, and copied into preference_conflicts so the narrative could name it. Preference fit is now four lists and no score, so the assertion moves rather than weakens: the .NET gate must appear in gate_hits and must NOT appear in preference_conflicts. Collapsing the two lists is the regression this case exists to prevent -- a disqualifier reading as one more dislike is exactly what the ceiling was compensating for.

other_flags: greenfield rewrite of a legacy load-planning system onto .NET 8

gate_hits.comment: The .NET hard gate is anti_pattern-typed, so it reads required_skills.

preference_conflicts.comment: The gate hit belongs to gate_hits and appears nowhere else. A hard gate and an ordinary matched negative are different kinds of finding, and the narrative reads them differently -- duplicating the row here would make one exclusion look like two objections of unequal weight.

preference_matches.comment: The rest of the role genuinely fits: logistics is the persona's strongest positive and the posting is remote and IC. A gate hit does not erase that, and with no score to average them into each other, both findings survive intact -- which is the whole reason the score went away.
